220 *Escherichia coli* lines underwent 36 days of mutation accumulation (MA), the time it takes to accumulate one mutation on average. The aim of the study was to estimate the distribution of fitness effects of new mutations (DFE) by measuring the growth rate of 188 of these MA lines and their common ancestor. Since the protocol also generated many lines that had accumulated no mutants, we could also estimate the distribution of fitness effects across genetically identical MA lines. We refer to this as the distribution of fitness effects due to environmental effects (EDFE) although acknowledge that we use the word 'environmental' to capture all systematic differences between lines not due to identified DNA mutations.

# Data

The 188 *Escherichia coli* mutation accumulation lines and four ancestral replicate lines were split into two sets, each containing 94 MA lines and 2 replicates of the ancestral line. For each set, the frozen lines (`line`) were grown while shaking for 16 hours at 37$^{\circ}$C in 10ml LB media, after which 10$\mu$L of culture was transferred to a 96-well filled with 190$\mu$L of LB.  Optical density measurements (`OD`) were taken every 5 minutes for four hours (`timepoint` in hours). This was repeated 14 times, and the membership of each set and the position of each line (`row` and `column`) on the `plate` was randomised between replicates.  The `date` on which the lines were defrosted and grown is recorded together with the `person` (JDH or DN) inoculating the cultures. JGS was responsible for inoculating all 96 well plates. 

```{r read_od}
library(dplyr)
library(gcplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

od_df<-read.csv(file.path(root, "meta/growth_data.csv"))
```

We can plot the optical density (OD) over time (with time jittered):

```{r plot_od}
plot(OD~jitter(timepoint,2), data=od_df, pch=16, cex=0.2, bty="l", ylab="Optical Density", xlab="Time (hours)")
```

While the bulk of the growth curves look reasonable, there are clearly some issues with no growth in some wells and some unusually high starting OD's. 

# Data filtering

## High starting OD 

There are `r sum(subset(od_df, timepoint==0.08)$OD>0.2)` replicates that have a starting OD higher than 0.2. 

```{r highOD}
od_df <- mutate(group_by(od_df, plate, row, column), startOD = OD[timepoint==0.08])
od_df$highOD<-od_df$startOD>0.2
tapply(od_df$highOD, od_df$plate, sum)/48
```

31 of these replicates were on plates 22 and 23. The function `plot_plate` allows us to visualise data in plate layout: 

<div class="fold s">
```{r plot_plate_fun}
plot_plate <- function(df, z, palette = "plasma", digits = 2) {

  ggplot(df, aes(x = as.factor(column), y = factor(row, levels=rev(LETTERS[1:8])), fill = df[[z]])) +
    geom_tile(colour = "grey50") +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(df[[z]], digits)),
              size = 3, colour = "white") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = palette, na.value = "white") +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(x = "Column", y = "Row", fill = z) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
}
```
</div>

We can see that wells with unusually high starting OD are clustered on the two plates: 

```{r plot_plate}
plot_plate(subset(od_df, timepoint==0.08 & plate==22), z = "OD")
plot_plate(subset(od_df, timepoint==0.08 & plate==23), z = "OD")
```

This does not look like systematic pipetting error, but rather some local issue with the plates.  Of the remaining seven wells with high starting OD, two were known to be due to pipetting error and were doubly inoculated (5-H-1 and 28-G-1 in red) and two were unintentionally blacked-out (2-A-8 and 1-A-5 in blue, see below)


```{r plot_od2}
plot(OD~jitter(timepoint,2), data=od_df, pch=16, cex=0.2, bty="l", ylab="Optical Density", xlab="Time (hours)")
points(OD~timepoint, data=subset(od_df, plate==5 & row=="H" & column==1), pch=16, cex=0.5, col="red")
points(OD~timepoint, data=subset(od_df, plate==28 & row=="G" & column==1), pch=16, cex=0.5, col="red")
points(OD~timepoint, data=subset(od_df, plate==2 & row=="A" & column==8), pch=16, cex=0.5, col="blue")
points(OD~timepoint, data=subset(od_df, plate==1 & row=="A" & column==5), pch=16, cex=0.5, col="blue")
```

For the remaining three wells (7-B-6, 28-B-4, 28-F-7) the starting OD was only a little above 0.2 and the growth curves look fine:

```{r plot_od2b}
plot(OD~timepoint, data=subset(od_df, highOD & plate%in%c(7,28) & row!="G"), pch=16, cex=0.5, bty="l", ylab="Optical Density", xlab="Time (hours)")
```

In order to retain these growth curves for later we will change their highOD flag to FALSE:

```{r }
with(od_df, highOD[which(highOD & plate%in%c(7,28) & row!="G")]<-FALSE)
```

## Empty wells

In 40 cases the initial culture looked like it hadn't grown, and in an error of judgement the culture was not assayed for growth and the well was either blacked-out (2-A-8 and 1-A-5, see above) or left empty (otherwise). 

```{r empty_wells}
plate.blank<-c(1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 11, 11, 15, 15, 15, 17, 19, 19, 21, 21, 21, 23, 23, 23, 25, 25, 27, 2, 8, 12, 18, 20, 22, 22, 22, 24, 24, 26, 28, 28, 28, 10, 10)
row.blank<-c("A", "A", "A", "B", "D", "H", "B", "D", "F", "F", "G", "H", "G", "B", "C", "A", "E", "F", "E", "F", "F", "C", "C", "D", "A", "C", "B", "F", "H", "A", "B", "H", "G", "F", "F", "C", "A", "E", "D", "H")
column.blank<-c(5, 8, 6, 3, 10, 5, 2, 3, 7, 6, 6, 12, 7, 12, 12, 6, 7, 8, 2, 2, 12, 2, 8, 2, 8, 12, 8, 4, 5, 8, 10, 10, 1, 1, 1, 2, 9, 9, 8, 12)
```

```{r }
od_df <- mutate(group_by(od_df, plate, row, column), empty = paste(plate, row, column)%in%paste(plate.blank, row.blank, column.blank))
```

```{r plot_empty_wells, echo=FALSE}
plot(OD~jitter(timepoint,2),data=subset(od_df, empty), pch=16, cex=0.2, bty="l", ylab="Optical Density", xlab="Time (hours)")
```

Note four (rather than two) wells do not appear empty - the additional wells are 22-H-10 and 23-F-2 for which there appeared to be an issue with the plate (see above). The number of empty wells per line is clearly overdispersed:

```{r }
n_empty<-tapply(od_df$empty, od_df$line, sum)/48
hist(n_empty, breaks=100, ylab="Number of Lines", xlab="Number of Empty Wells")
```

In particular line `r names(n_empty)[which.max(n_empty)]` repeatedly failed to grow (`r max(n_empty)` times out of 14).

```{r }
n_empty[which(n_empty!=0)]
```

## Extra wells

In addition, well 5-F-9 also appears empty. This replicate was of line `r subset(od_df, plate==5 & row=="F" & column==9)$line[1]` which repeatedly failed to grow (see above).

```{r }
od_df <- mutate(group_by(od_df, plate, row, column), extra_empty = OD[timepoint==2]<0.2 & !empty)
plot(OD~jitter(timepoint,2), data=od_df, pch=16, cex=0.2, bty="l", ylab="Optical Density", xlab="Time (hours)")
points(OD~timepoint, data=subset(od_df, extra_empty), pch=16, cex=0.5, col="red")
```

Nevertheless, three replicates of line 180 did grow despite starting at a low OD:

```{r plot_empty_wells2, echo=FALSE}
plot(OD~jitter(timepoint,2),data=subset(od_df, !empty & !extra_empty), pch=16, cex=0.2, bty="l", ylab="Optical Density", xlab="Time (hours)")
points(OD~timepoint, data=subset(od_df, line=="180"), pch=16, cex=0.5, col="red")
```

## Filtering

In what follows we remove empty wells and those in which the starting OD was greater than 0.2 (except 7-B-6, 28-B-4 and 28-F-7 which look fine):

```{r }
od_df <- subset(od_df, !highOD & !empty & !extra_empty)
```

```{r plot_OD_noproblems}
plot(OD~jitter(timepoint,2),data=od_df, pch=16, cex=0.2, bty="l", ylab="Optical Density", xlab="Time (hours)")
```

# Growth rate and meta data

In order to get an estimate of the growth rate in the exponential phase we can use gcplyr [@Blazanin.2024]. The change in log OD is computed over consecutive time-points for each well and a rolling 3-timepoint average calculated:  

```{r growth_rate, eval=rerun.r}
df <- mutate(group_by(od_df, plate, row, column), deriv = calc_deriv(x = timepoint, y = OD, percapita = TRUE, blank = 0, window_width_n = 3, trans_y = 'log'))
```

For each well, the maximum average change is taken as the growth rate:

```{r sum_growth_rate, eval=rerun.r}
df <- summarize(df, r = max_gc(deriv), across(-c(timepoint, OD, deriv),first))
```

Since growth rates may be different in the inner wells, we can create a factor for modelling this

```{r inner, eval=rerun.r}
df <- mutate(df, inner = as.numeric(!(row %in% c('A', 'H') | column %in% c(1, 12))))
```

`scripts/Mutation_Calling.Rmd` details the pipeline in which mutations were identified, and the number of mutations per line can be added:

```{r number_mutations}
mutations<-read.csv(file.path(root, "meta/real_mutations.csv"))
```

```{r }
nmutations<-table(factor(mutations$line, levels=unique(df$line)))
df$mutation<-as.numeric(nmutations[df$line])
```

and have two indicator variables for whether a line is the ancestor (`anc`) or not (`noanc`):

```{r anc-noanc}
df$anc<-as.numeric(df$line=="anc")
df$noanc<-as.numeric(df$line!="anc")
```

A violin plot of the growth rates reveals an outlier with a very high growth rate:

```{r plot_gr}
ggplot(data=df,aes(x='',y=r)) + geom_violin() + geom_boxplot(width=0.1)+scale_y_continuous(name="growth rate")
```

It seems that the high growth rate is driven by the anomalous OD readings (in red)

```{r anomalous_OD}
plot(log(OD)~timepoint, data=subset(od_df, plate==23 & row=="H" & column==1), ylab="log(OD)", xlab="Time (hours)")
points(log(OD)~timepoint, data=subset(od_df, plate==23 & row=="H" & column==1 & timepoint>1.55 & timepoint<1.7), col="red", pch=16, cex=1.25)
```

Consequently, we also remove this data point:

```{r rm_anomalous_OD}
df<-subset(df, r<1.5)
```

Line 95 accumulated a mutation in the mismatch-repair gene MutL and consequently had an elevated mutation rate with `r sum(mutations$line==95)` fixed mutations observed. There is evidence from the sequencing data that an addition five mutations arose after mutation accumulation but prior to sequencing. Given new mutations are also likely to arise during the growth assay, and data from this line are likely to have high leverage (all other lines had between zero and five), we removed this line from the analysis:

```{r rm_95}
df<-subset(df, line!=95)
```

## Empty wells

40 replicates were not assayed because the initial culture looked like it hadn't grown, with  certain lines being overrepresented. If the initial culture did not grow because of the accumulated mutations in the line, this will bias our estimates of the DFE. However, if we compare the growth rates of lines where at least one replicates was excluded with the growth rates of lines where no replicates were excluded the difference is small and non-significant:


```{r }
nz_empty<-n_empty[which(n_empty!=0)]
summary(lm(r~as.factor(line%in%nz_empty), data=df))
```

Indeed, if we plot the growth rates of the four lines with the most replicates excluded (the coloured points) they do not obviously grow more slowly than other lines:

```{r excluded_plot}
boxplot(r~as.factor(line%in%nz_empty), data=df, ylab="Growth Rate", xlab="At least one replicate excluded")

worst_four<-subset(df, line%in%names(nz_empty)[which(nz_empty>4)])

points(r~I(2+(as.numeric(as.factor(line))-2.5)/6), col=as.numeric(as.factor(line)), data=worst_four)
```

and the line (in red) with the lowest average growth rate actually has no mutations:

```{r }
with(worst_four, mutation[match(levels(as.factor(line)), line)])
```

# Models

## Main model

We fit a linear mixed model to the maximum growth rates with the aim of estimating the mean and variance of the distribution of fitness effects of new mutations (DFE) and the environment experienced by a line (EDFE). 

```{r m1}
library(lmerTest)

m1<-lmer(r~mutation + anc + person + inner + (noanc-1|line) + (sqrt(mutation)-1|line) + (1|plate) + (1|plate:column) + (1|plate:row), data=df)
```

The basic biological model is:

\begin{equation}
r_{ij} = \beta_0+\delta^{(A)}_i\beta_A+n_i\beta_M+(1-\delta^{(A)}_i)u^{(E)}_i+\sqrt{n_i}u^{(M)}_i+e_{ij}$$
\end{equation}

where $r_{ij}$ is the maximum growth rate of replicate $j$ from line $i$. When the line is an ancestral line, $\delta^{(A)}$ (`anc`) is one but is zero for MA lines. $n_i$ (`mutation`) is the number of called mutations that may be zero even for MA lines.

 The fixed effects are

* $\beta_0$ is the expected growth rate of a zero-mutant MA line: `(Intercept)`
* $\beta_M$ is the linear change in fitness per mutation, related to the mean of the DFE: `mutation`.
* $\beta_A$ is the effect of a line being an ancestor: `anc`

 The random effects are

* $u^{(M)}_i$ is the average effect of each mutation in MA line $i$. The variance of these effects ($\sigma^2_M$) is related to the variance of the DFE:  `(sqrt(mutation)-1|line)`
* $u^{(E)}_i$ is the expected effect of MA line $i$ had the number of new mutations been zero. The variance of these effects is the variance of the EDFE ($\sigma^2_E$): `(noanc-1|line)`
* $e_{ij}$ the residual for replicate $j$ of $i$ with variance $\sigma^2_e$.

We also control for technical variation.  The fixed effects are

* `person`: effect of the person inoculating the cultures.
* `inner`: effect of whether growth rates are different in inner wells. 

 The random effects are

* `(1|plate)`: effect of being on a specific plate. 
* `(1|plate:column)`: effect of being in a specific column of a specific plate.
* `(1|plate:row)`"" effect of being in a specific row of a specific plate.

The model summary is:

```{r m1_summary}
summary(m1)
```

The biological findings of this model are:

* Assuming no cell death, we can divide $ln(2)$ by the intercept to get an estimate of the generation time of a mutant-free line (grown in an outer well and inoculated by DN): `r round(60*log(2)/fixef(m1)["(Intercept)"])`  minutes.

* The `mutation` effect is the change in log growth rate caused by a single mutation $\beta_M$- it is small and not significantly different from zero.

* The `anc` effect ($\beta_A$) is positive suggesting that the ancestral line grows faster than the average growth rate of the mutant-free lines.  

* The `line.1` (`noanc`) variance, $\sigma^2_E$, $which is due to between-line differences not caused by mutations, explains approximately  `r round(100*VarCorr(m1)$line.1/(sum(unlist(VarCorr(m1)))+sigma(m1)^2))`\% of the total variance (after controlling for the fixed effects).   

* The estimate of the `line` (`sqrt(mutation)`) variance, $\sigma^2_M$, is bound at zero and suggests that single mutations generate very little, if any, between-line variance. 

We can use the DHARMa package to assess the model fit: 

```{r }
library(DHARMa)
simres<-simulateResiduals(m1)
plot(simres)
``` 

While there are significant deviations from expectation, the magnitude of the deviations are rather small. 

We can also plot the data and some model predictions in order to get a feel for what the model is telling us

<div class="fold s">
```{r main_plot,  fig.width = 7,fig.height = 10, fig.cap="Raw growth rate (log(OD) per hour) for lines grouped by number of accumulated mutations. Replicates of non-ancestral lines are in orange and replicates of ancestral lines are in blue. The solid black line is the fitted regression with black dots representing the predicted mean fitness for lines with different numbers of mutation. The whiskers indicate the 95\\% quantiles for the line effects (full black bars) and the observations (dashed black bars). The cyan data point is the estimated mean ancestral growth rate."}

intercept=fixef(m1)['(Intercept)']
mutation_effect=fixef(m1)['mutation']
ancestor_effect=fixef(m1)['anc']

env_variance<-as.numeric(VarCorr(m1)[['line.1']])
tech_variance<-as.numeric(VarCorr(m1)[['plate.column']]+VarCorr(m1)[['plate.row']]+VarCorr(m1)[['plate']])
mut_variance<-as.numeric(VarCorr(m1)[['line']])
res_variance<-sigma(m1)^2

pred_mutations<-0:3

pred_mean<-intercept+mutation_effect*pred_mutations
pred_var<-env_variance+res_variance+mut_variance*pred_mutations+tech_variance
pred_bl_var<-env_variance+mut_variance*pred_mutations

pred_ancestor<-intercept+ancestor_effect

pred_lower_q<-qnorm(0.025,pred_mean,sqrt(pred_var))
pred_upper_q<-qnorm(0.975,pred_mean,sqrt(pred_var))

pred_lower_q_bl<-qnorm(0.025,pred_mean,sqrt(pred_bl_var))
pred_upper_q_bl<-qnorm(0.975,pred_mean,sqrt(pred_bl_var))

plot_data<-cbind(pred_mutations,pred_mean,pred_lower_q,pred_upper_q,pred_lower_q_bl,pred_upper_q_bl)

df_plot <- df %>% 
  mutate(point_col = case_when(
    noanc == 0                          ~ "blue",
    mutation <= 3 & noanc == 1          ~ "orange",
    TRUE                                ~ "other")
  )

df_plot<-df_plot[order(df_plot$point_col, decreasing=TRUE),]

CI <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(pred_mutations, pred_mean)) +

  ## a) raw-data points (jittered) -------------
  geom_jitter(data = filter(df_plot, point_col != "other"),
              aes(x = mutation, y = r, colour = point_col),
              width  = .20, height = 0, alpha = .5, show.legend = FALSE) +

  scale_colour_manual(values = c(orange = "darkorange",
                                 blue   = "darkblue")) +

  ## b) regression line ------------------------
  geom_abline(intercept = intercept, slope = mutation_effect) +

  ## c) fitted means & error bars --------------
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = pred_upper_q, ymax = pred_lower_q),
                width = .5, colour = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = pred_upper_q_bl, ymax = pred_lower_q_bl),
                width = .5, colour = "black") +

  ## d) ancestor point -------------------------
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = pred_ancestor, colour = "cyan", size = 3, alpha = 1)+

  ## e) axes, labels, limits -------------------
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-.5, 3.5),
                     name   = "Number of mutations") +
  ylab("Growth rate") +

  ## f) theme ----------------------------------
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
 #   axis.text   = element_text(face = "bold"),
   axis.title  = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10, r = 20, b = 20))
  )

  plot(CI)
  if(save){
  ggsave(file.path(root,'models/fitness.jpeg'),width = 5, height = 4,units='in')
  }
```
</div>

There seems to be quite a few reduced growth rates in the single mutant class - many of these are associated with line 45 which has a frameshift mutation in the *SspA* gene:

## Obtaining the DFE 

The previous model provides a model for the growth rates of each line. However, 
to obtain the DFE we need to compute the distribution of relative fitnesses for single-mutant lines compared to zero-mutant lines. The expected growth rate of single-mutant lines ($r_w$) is the intercept, $\beta_0$.

\begin{equation}
r_w = \beta_0
\end{equation}

The expected growth rate of line $i$ is

\begin{equation}
r_i = \beta_0 + n_i\beta_M+\sqrt{n_i}u^{(M)}_i
\end{equation}

where the expectation is taken over the distribution of environmental effects. 

The selection coefficient for MA line $i$ is $r_i-r_w$, although this is in units *per hour* and is therefore hard to compare across studies and species (See Equation 2.2 in @Chevin.2011b and Equation 7 in  @Fink.2024). To make selection coefficients more comparable, they can be put on the scale of generations by using Equation 3.2 in @Chevin.2011b:

\begin{equation}
s_i=\frac{r_i-r_w}{r_w}ln(2)
\end{equation}


Setting $n=1$, the distribution of generation-scaled fitness effects (the DFE) from our model is normal with mean 

\begin{equation}
\mu_s  = \frac{\beta_M}{\beta_0}ln(2)
\end{equation}

and variance 

\begin{equation}
\sigma^2_s  = \frac{\sigma^2_M}{\beta_0^2}ln(2)^2
\end{equation}


Since the mean and the variance of the DFE are functions of model parameters we refit model `m1` using Markov chain Monte Carlo in order to obtain credible intervals. 


```{r mcmc, eval=rerun.mcmc}
library(MCMCglmm)

m1_mcmc<-MCMCglmm(r~mutation+anc+person+inner, 
                  random=~line+idh(sqrt(mutation)):line+plate+plate:column+plate:row, 
                  data=as.data.frame(df), 
                  prior=list(R=IW(1, 0.002), G=F(1,1000)), 
                  longer=10, verbose=FALSE)

```

The model estimates are very close to those obtained using restricted maximum likelihood:

```{r }   
summary(m1_mcmc)
```

We can obtain the posterior distributions for the mean and variance of the DFE

```{r }
mean_s<-log(2)*m1_mcmc$Sol[,"mutation"]/m1_mcmc$Sol[,"(Intercept)"]

mean(mean_s)
HPDinterval(mean_s)

var_s<-(log(2)^2)*m1_mcmc$VCV[,"sqrt(mutation).line"]/m1_mcmc$Sol[,"(Intercept)"]^2

mean(var_s)
HPDinterval(var_s)
```

### Estimating the DFE using the ancestor as a reference

Most studies do not have zero-mutant lines to which they can compare the fitness of lines carrying mutations. This is only valid if all between-line variance is due to mutations.  If we had used the ancestor as the reference then

\begin{equation}
r_w = \beta_0+\beta_A
\end{equation}

where $\beta_A$ is the effect of the ancestor. The mean and variance of the DFE would then be:

\begin{equation}
%\mu_s = \frac{\beta_0+\beta_M-\beta_0-\beta_A}{\beta_0+\beta_A}ln(2)
\mu_s = \frac{\beta_M-\beta_A}{\beta_0+\beta_A}ln(2)
\end{equation}

and 

\begin{equation}
\sigma^2_s  = \frac{\sigma^2_M}{(\beta_0+\beta_A)^2}ln(2)^2
\end{equation}

which gives


```{r }
mean_s2<-log(2)*(m1_mcmc$Sol[,"mutation"]-m1_mcmc$Sol[,"anc"])/(m1_mcmc$Sol[,"(Intercept)"]+m1_mcmc$Sol[,"anc"])

mean(mean_s2)
HPDinterval(mean_s2)

var_s2<-(log(2)^2)*m1_mcmc$VCV[,"sqrt(mutation).line"]/(m1_mcmc$Sol[,"(Intercept)"]+m1_mcmc$Sol[,"anc"])^2

mean(var_s2)
HPDinterval(var_s2)
```

## Is the ancestor effect comparable to other zero-mutant line effects? 

The ancestor's growth rate is estimated to be `r round(fixef(m1)["anc"],4)` units larger than the average growth rate of the zero-mutant lines. However, the zero-mutant lines are not equivalent and vary to some degree in their growth rate - the estimated standard deviation (the square-root of the `line` variance) is `r round(sqrt(VarCorr(m1)["line.1"][[1]]), 4)`. Since `r round(fixef(m1)["anc"],4)`/`r round(sqrt(VarCorr(m1)["line.1"][[1]]), 4)` = `r round(fixef(m1)["anc"]/sqrt(VarCorr(m1)["line.1"][[1]]), 3)` it is not an outlier with respect to the distribution of zero-mutant line effects. We can test this formally by fitting a random line effect for the ancestor that comes from the same distribution as the zero-mutant line effects. The fixed ancestral effect is now smaller and no longer significant:

```{r m2}
m2<-lmer(r ~ mutation + anc + person + inner + (1|line) + (sqrt(mutation)-1|line) + (1|plate) + (1|plate:column) + (1|plate:row), data=df)
summary(m2)
```

## Mutation type

In the previous models all mutations are treated as being equivalent. However, we might expect synonymous mutations and small structural mutations in non-coding regions to have negligible fitness effects compared to other mutations. We can count the number of mutations per line that are not of this type (`nsyn_mutation`)

```{r nsyn_mutations}
nsyn_mutations<-subset(mutations, (nchar(REF)!=nchar(ALT) & coding) | ALT=="<DEL>" | type%in%c("nonsynonymous", "nonsense", "frameshift"))
nnsyn_mutations<-table(factor(nsyn_mutations$line, levels=unique(df$line)))
df$nsyn_mutation<-as.numeric(nnsyn_mutations[df$line])
```

and rerun model with this as a predictor

```{r m3}
m3<-lmer(r ~ nsyn_mutation + anc + person + inner + (noanc-1|line) + (sqrt(nsyn_mutation)-1|line) + (1|plate) + (1|plate:column) + (1|plate:row),data=df)
summary(m3)
```

We find that even when we only look at mutations that likely have a stronger effect on fitness, mutations do not significantly influence growth rate. 

## Can the between-line variance be explained by variation in starting OD?

A common practice when measuring bacterial growth curves is to standardize the inoculation cell density to minimize any influence of starting density on growth curve parameter estimates. While this what not feasible given the level of throughput, we can attempt to control for starting density (`startOD`) statistically. However, there is the danger that we control for some of the fitness variation we seek to measure if the fast growth of a line results in high starting density.  

```{r m4}
m4<-lmer(r ~ mutation + anc + person + inner + startOD + (noanc-1|line) + (sqrt(mutation)-1|line) + (1|plate) + (1|plate:column) + (1|plate:row),data=df)
summary(m4)
```

The effect of starting density on the maximum growth rate is small and non-significant, and the impact on other model parameters is negligible.

## Significance testing of random effect variances

To test the significance of the fixed effects we use t-tests with the degrees of freedom obtained using the Satterthwaite approximation as implemented in `lmerTest`. To test the significance of the random effects we perform likelihood ratio tests implemented in the $\texttt{anova}$ method for lmer objects (although we note that the p-values could be halved [@Chernoff.1954]).

### Genetic line effects

We can omit the term `(sqrt(mutation)-1|line)` from model `m1` to test whether the variance of the DFE is non-zero


```{r m5}
m5<-lmer(r ~ mutation + anc + person + inner + (noanc-1|line) + (1|plate) + (1|plate:column) + (1|plate:row),data=df)
anova(m5,m1)
```

The evidence is not strong

### Environmental line effects

We can omit the term `(noanc-1|line)` from model `m1` to test whether the variance of the EDFE is non-zero

```{r m6}
m6<-lmer(r ~ mutation + anc + person + inner + (sqrt(mutation)-1|line) + (1|plate) + (1|plate:column) + (1|plate:row),data=df)
anova(m6,m1)
```

There is strong evidence that lines vary in their fitness due to things other than the mutations they've accumulated.

```{r m7, echo=FALSE}
m7<-lmer(r ~ mutation + anc + person + inner  + (1|plate) + (1|plate:column) + (1|plate:row),data=df)
# additional analysis for performing LRT on the total between-line variance
```

# Comparison with @Sane.2018

@Sane.2018 also used an MA procedure where lines differ by single mutations. However, rather than running many lines for a short period of time and sequencing at the end, they ran few lines for a long period and sequenced them periodically. Consequently, rather than comparing MA lines with a common unmutated ancestor, each line is compared to its ancestor prior to the accumulation of a single mutation.  In total, 80 single mutations were assayed.  

```{r inputSane}
df_long_Sane<-read.csv(file.path(root, "meta/Sane_data.csv"))
```

The data frame was kindly provided by Mrudula Sane and Deepa Agashe and contains three columns `abs_gr_1`, `abs_gr_2`, `abs_gr_3` which are the three replicate growth rate estimates for each line.  `cognate_anc_gr` is the estimated growth rate of that line's immediate ancestor (presumably the average of three replicates). The `rel_gr` column is the relative growth rate as used in the paper which is the average value of the `abs_gr` variables,  divided by `cognate_anc_gr` (note this is equal to $1+(r_i-r_w)/r_w$).

We can turn this wide-format data-frame into long format with the three absolute growth rates appearing in the single column (`r`):


```{r }
df_Sane <- df_long_Sane[,c('mutation_id',"abs_gr_1", "abs_gr_2", "abs_gr_3","cognate_anc_gr", "transfer")] %>%
    pivot_longer(
        cols = c("abs_gr_1", "abs_gr_2", "abs_gr_3"),
        names_to = "replicate",
        values_to = "r"
    )
```

Ideally, we would have information of the replicate estimates that formed each `cognate_anc_gr` in order to model uncertainty in $r_w$. It would also have been good to know the line identity of the immediate ancestor, since the line may itself have acquired a single mutation from a more distant ancestor. Since this information is not available we will analyse $ln(2)(r_m-r_w)/r_w$

```{r SaneFitness_model}
df_Sane=df_Sane %>% mutate(s =log(2)*(r-cognate_anc_gr)/cognate_anc_gr)

m1_Sane<-lmer(s~(1|mutation_id),data=df_Sane)
```

```{r SaneSummary}
summary(m1_Sane)
```

The mean of the DFE (the intercept) exceeds zero by some margin and the variance of the DFE is also substantial and highly significant:

```{r }
m0_Sane<-lm(s~1,data=df_Sane)
anova(m1_Sane, m0_Sane)
```

 Part of the between-line variance will be driven by the fact that the same `cognate_anc_gr` value is used for each of the three replicate growth rates of a mutation. However, if we analyse the replicate growth rates of each line without normalising by the ancestors growth rate and generation time we still see substantial between-line variance. 

```{r SaneFitness_model2}
m2_Sane<-lmer(r~(1|mutation_id),data=df_Sane)
```

```{r SaneSummary2}
summary(m2_Sane)
```

We can also fit the model `m1_Sane` using Markov chain Monte Carlo:

```{r sane_coefficient}

m1_Sane_mcmc<-MCMCglmm(s~1, 
                       random=~mutation_id, 
                       data=df_Sane, 
                       prior=list(R=IW(1,0.002), G=F(1,1000)), 
                       longer=10,
                      verbose=FALSE) 

summary(m1_Sane_mcmc)
```

# Hidden mutations

We interpret our estimate of $\sigma^2_E$ (the variance associated with the `(noanc - 1 | line)` term) as the variance due to non-genetic effects. This would clearly be compromised if mutations were present in our putatively zero-mutation lines. Putatively zero-mutation lines may harbour mutations because of false-negative mutation calling, sample mix-ups and/or new mutations that arose after sequencing. 

## Mutation calling errors and mix-ups

In `scripts/Mutation_Calling.Rmd` we simulated mutations and assessed how often our pipeline failed to call it. We found that 196/196 bps, 194/196 deletions and 192/196 insertions were detected. 17 of our INDELS were deletions and 7 were insertions. Consequently, the true number of INDELS is expected to be 17/(194/196)+7/(192/196)=`r round(17/(194/196)+7/(192/196), 2)`: our best estimate is that we missed `r round(17/(194/196)+7/(192/196)-24, 2)` mutations in total and on average around `r round(17/(194/196)+7/(192/196)-24, 2)` /188= `r round((17/(194/196)+7/(192/196)-24)/188, 4)` mutations per assayed line. We also resequenced twenty-two lines in order to assess whether there had been any mix-ups. One of the twenty-two lines had switched identity between sequencing and resequencing, suggesting a mix-up rate of $p_M=$ 1/22=`r round(1/22,3)`. The number of false-positives is hard to assess, but given the resequencing confirmed all mutations called in the original sequencing, the false-positive rate is likely very low. The average number of called mutations per line will then be close to the expected number of true positives which is 202/188=`r round(202/188, 3)` among assayed lines. 

To understand how omitted mutations contribute to the between line variance in putatively zero-mutant lines we can think about the number of omitted mutations, $\mathscr{O}$, in line $i$:

\begin{equation}
\mathscr{O}_i=(1-\delta)n^{(fn)}_{i}+\delta(n^{(tp)}_{j}+n^{(fn)}_{j})
\end{equation}

where $n^{(fn)}$ and $n^{(tp)}$ are the number of false-negative and true-positive mutations in a line, and $\delta=1$ if line $i$ has been mixed up with line $j$ but is zero otherwise. Line $j$ is assumed to be a line drawn at random from all lines. The effect of these omitted mutations on a line's fitness is:

\begin{equation}
u^{(\mathscr{O})}_i=\sum_k^{\mathscr{O}_i} \beta_M+u^{(M)}_k
\end{equation}

If we take the expectation of this random sum we get the contribution of omitted mutations to the mean fitness of putatively zero-mutant lines

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rl}
\beta_{\mathscr{O}}=&\beta_mE[\mathscr{O}]\\
                    =&\beta_m\left((1-p_m)E[n^{(fn)}]+p_m(E[n^{(tp)}]+E[n^{(fn)}])\right)\\
                    =&\beta_m\left(E[n^{(fn)}]+p_mE[n^{(tp)}]\right)\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}

If we take the variance of the random sum we get the contribution of omitted mutations to the variance in fitness of putatively zero-mutant lines. Assuming the number of omitted mutations is independent of their effect, we can use the Blackwell-Girshick equation [@Blackwell.1979]:

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rl}
\sigma^2_{\mathscr{O}}=&VAR(\mathscr{O})E[\beta_M+u^{(M)}]^2+E[\mathscr{O}]VAR(\beta_M+u^{(M)})\\
                      =&VAR(\mathscr{O})\beta_M^2+E[\mathscr{O}]\sigma^2_M\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}


$VAR(\mathscr{O})$ can be obtained using the law of total variance:

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rl}
VAR(\mathscr{O}) =& E[VAR(\mathscr{O} | \delta)]+VAR(E[\mathscr{O} | \delta])\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}

Assuming $n^{(tp)}$ and $n^{(fn)}$ are drawn from independent Poisson distributions then $E[\mathscr{O} | \delta=0]=VAR(\mathscr{O} | \delta=0)=E[n^{(fn)}]$ and $E[\mathscr{O} | \delta=1]=VAR(\mathscr{O} | \delta=1)=E[n^{(tp)}]+E[n^{(fn)}]$ to give:


\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rl}
VAR(\mathscr{O}) =& E[n^{(fn)}]+p_mE[n^{(tp)}]+p_m(1-p_M)E[n^{(tp)}]^2\\
                 =& E[\mathscr{O}]+p_m(1-p_M)E[n^{(tp)}]^2\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}

and so

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rl}
\sigma^2_{\mathscr{O}}=&(E[n^{(fn)}]+p_mE[n^{(tp)}])(\beta_M^2+\sigma^2_M)+p_m(1-p_M)E[n^{(tp)}]^2\beta_M^2\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}


```{r echo=FALSE}
Efn<-(17/(194/196)+7/(192/196)-24)/188
Efp<-Efn
Etp<-202/188
p_m<-1/22
rho<-(1-p_m)*Etp/(Etp+Efp)
tau<-60
mu_g<-0.00105
```

Using our estimates of $E[n^{(fn)}]$=`r round(Efn, 4)`, $E[n^{(tp)}]$=`r round(Etp, 4)` and $p_m$=`r round(p_m,4)` we get $\beta_{\mathscr{O}}=\beta_m$ `r round(Efn+p_m*Etp, 4)` and $\sigma^2_{\mathscr{O}}=\sigma^2_M$ `r round(Efn+p_m*Etp, 4)` $+\beta_M^2$ `r round(Efn+p_m*Etp+(1-p_m)*p_m*Etp^2, 4)`.

## New mutations

In the final round of MA a colony is grown from a single initial cell up to approximately x cells, this colony is frozen, and a sub-sample is taken and grown ..... Any mutation present in the initial cell will be called. Any new mutations that appear as the final colony grows, or between stock and sequencing, are extremely unlikely to be called since they would only be found in a small proportion of cells. However, new mutations that appear in the final colony, or between the final colony and the fitness assay stock, may in aggregate cause the fitness of the line to differ systematically from a zero-mutant line. Note that mutations that appear in each replicate after growing from the common stock will only contribute to the within-line (residual) variance and do not need to be considered.

If we have $N_c$ as the number of cells in the final colony, and $N_1$ the number of cells which initiated the stock and $N_2$ the final number of cells in the stock, the number of cell divisions experienced by a cell is $\tau=log_2(N_c)+log_2(N_2)-log_2(N_1)$ assuming synchronous growth. From our MA lines the mutation rate per genome per generation was estimated to be $\mu_g=0.00105$ (see \citet{Lee2012RateSequencing} also) such that the expected number of mutations per line is $\tau\mu_g$. $log_2(N_c)$ is approximately 28 \citet{Lee2012RateSequencing} and $log_2(N_2)-log_2(N_1)$ is approximately 32 such that $\tau\mu_g=$ `r round(tau*mu_g,3)`. If the number of mutations per cell is Poisson distributed only a small proportion of cells will have new mutations  $1-e^{-\tau\mu_g}=$ `r round(1-exp(-tau*mu_g),3)` and of those, `r round(100*dpois(1, tau*mu_g)/(1-dpois(0, tau*mu_g)))`\% will only carry a single mutation. Note the average number of cell divisions experienced by cells in the final colony will exceed $log_2(N_c)$ since colony growth is asymmetric [@Gralka.2016] which will mean $\tau$ is underestimated and $\mu_g$ is overestimated since $log_2(N_c)$ is used to convert the number of accumulated mutations into a rate per generation [@GrosseSommer.2026a]. 

To understand how these new mutations contribute to the between line variance we can think about the number of new mutations (as opposed to the number of mutants) in a line, $\mathscr{M}$, and the number of cells that carry each of those mutations, a mutation's clone size. For new mutation $k$, the clone size is $NP_k$ where N is the total number of cells and $P_k$ the proportion of cells that carry mutation $k$.  The aggregate effect of new mutations on line $i$'s fitness is then a sum of each mutations fitness effect ($\beta_M+u^{(M)}_k$) weighted by the frequency of that mutation, $P_k$:

$$u^{(\mathscr{M})}_i=\sum^\mathscr{M}_k P_k(\beta_M+u^{(M)}_k)$$

 The variance of this sum across lines is the contribution of new mutations to the between-line variance in putatively zero-mutant lines, which we will designate as $\sigma^2_\mathscr{M}$. The variance of this sum can be approximated by the Blackwell-Girshick equation [@Blackwell.1979]. 

$$\sigma^2_\mathscr{M}=E[\mathscr{M}]VAR(P(\beta_M+u^{(M)}))+E[P(\beta_M+u^{(M)})]^2VAR(\mathscr{M})$$

It is only approximate because the number of mutations in a line cannot be independent of the proportions, but the approximation should work well when mutations are rare. Under a neutral model, $P$ and $\beta_M+u^{(M)}$ are uncorrelated and so the variance of $P(\beta_M+u^{(M)})$ is $VAR(P)\sigma^2_M+\sigma^2_ME[P]^2+VAR(P)\beta_M^2$. Putting this together we have,

$$\sigma^2_\mathscr{M}=E[\mathscr{M}][VAR(P)\sigma^2_M+\sigma^2_ME[P]^2+VAR(P)\beta_M^2]+E[P]^2\beta_M^2VAR(\mathscr{M})$$. 

If mutations arise from a Poisson process then $VAR(\mathscr{M})=E[\mathscr{M}]$ and we get

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rl}
\sigma^2_\mathscr{M}=&E[\mathscr{M}](VAR(P)+E[P]^2)(\sigma^2_M+\beta_M^2)\\
                    =&E[\mathscr{M}]E[P^2](\sigma^2_M+\beta_M^2)\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}

@Lea.1949 give the probability mass function for a mutation's clone size under synchronous growth given the total population size:

$$Pr(PN=\nu | N)=\frac{1}{\nu(\nu+1)}$$. 

Since $PN$ cannot exceed $N$ we can compute

$$E[(PN)^2 | N] = \int_0^N\nu^2\frac{1}{\nu(\nu+1)}d\nu= N-ln(N+1)$$

such that $E[P^2]=\frac{1}{N}-\frac{ln(N+1)}{N^2}$ and

$$\sigma^2_\mathscr{M}=E[\mathscr{M}]\left(\frac{1}{N}-\frac{ln(N+1)}{N^2}\right)(\sigma^2_M+\beta_M^2)$$

In a population of $N$ cells there has been $N$ fission events which means $E[\mathscr{M}]=N\mu_g$ where $\mu_g$ is the number of mutations per genome per generation. The contribution of new mutations to the between-line variance is therefore: 

$$\sigma^2_\mathscr{M}=\mu_g\left(1-\frac{ln(N+1)}{N}\right)(\sigma^2_M+\beta_M^2)$$

Since $ln(N+1)/N$ is so much smaller than one when $N$ is large this is approximately

$$\sigma^2_\mathscr{M}\approx\mu_g[\sigma^2_M+\beta_M^2]$$

Perhaps surprisingly, the contribution of new mutations to the between-line variance does not depend on the total number of cells and therefore the number of generations that have elapsed, $\tau$. The effect of new mutations on the mean fitness of zero-mutant lines, however, does depends on $N$ and therefore $\tau$. Given the expected number of mutations per cell us $\mu_g\tau$, the contribution of the new mutations to the expected fitness in putatively zero-mutant lines is

$$\beta_\mathscr{M}=\beta_M\mu_g\tau$$

We can also derive this using the results of @Lea.1949:

$$\beta_\mathscr{M}=E[u^{(\mathscr{M})}]=\beta_ME[\mathscr{M}]E[P]$$

Since 

$$E[PN | N] = \int_0^N\nu\frac{1}{\nu(\nu+1)}d\nu= ln(N+1)$$

we get

$$\beta_\mathscr{M}=\beta_MN\mu_g\frac{ln(N+1)}{N}=\beta_M\mu_gln(N+1)$$. 

This differs from $\beta_M\mu_g\tau$ by approximately a factor $ln(2)$. This is likely due to the Lea–Coulson approximation assuming mutant cells grow stochastically according to a Yule process rather than deterministic synchronous growth.  

Using our estimates of $\mu_g$ =`r round(mu_g, 5)` and $\tau$=`r round(tau,2)` we get $\beta_{\mathscr{O}}=\beta_m$ `r round(tau*mu_g, 4)` and $\sigma^2_{\mathscr{O}}=\sigma^2_M$ `r round(mu_g, 4)`.


We can check these results through simulation. `sim_new` is a function that simulates a population that doubles `tau` times. At each cell division the two sister cells acquire mutations sampled from a Poisson with mean `mu_g`. The mutations add an increment to the cell's original fitness with the increments sample from a normal with mean `b_M` and variance `s2_M`:

<div class="fold s">
```{r sim_new}

sim_new<-function(tau, mu_g, b_M, s2_M){

  N<-2^tau
  w<-rep(0, N)

  for(j in 1:tau){

      Njm1<-2^(j-1)
      w[Njm1+1:Njm1]<-w[1:Njm1]  # assign 'parent' fitness to 'offspring'

      nmu<-rpois(1, mu_g*2^j)      # determine total number of mutations
      
      if(nmu>0){
        mu_pos<-sample(1:(2^j), nmu) 
        # determine the cells in which mutations happen (note double mutants not allowed)
        
        w[mu_pos]<-w[mu_pos]+rnorm(nmu, b_M, sqrt(s2_M))
        # update cell's fitness
      }

  }
  return(w)
}  
```
</div>

We can take the average fitness of cells in a line, and by simulating a large number of lines (2,000) that have been propagated for varying numbers of generations ($\tau$ from 1 to 25) we can compute the relevant measures ($\beta_\mathscr{M}$, $\sigma^2_\mathscr{M}$, $E[P]$ and $E[P^2]$) and compare them against the theoretical expectations. We use $\mu_g=0.001$, $\beta_M=0.1$ and $\sigma^2_M=1$:

```{r eval=!rerun.newsim, echo=FALSE}
mu_g_sim<-0.001
b_M_sim<-0.1
s2_M_sim<-1
load(file.path(root,'models/newsim.Rdata'))
```

<div class="fold s">
```{r newsim,  eval=rerun.newsim}

max_tau<-25
nlines<-2000
mu_g_sim<-0.001
b_M_sim<-0.1
s2_M_sim<-1

newsim<-matrix(NA, max_tau, 5)
colnames(newsim)<-c("tau", "Ew", "Vw", "EP", "EP2")
newsim[,"tau"]<-1:max_tau

for(tau in 1:max_tau){

    res<-matrix(NA, nlines, 4)
    colnames(res)<-c("Ew", "EP", "EP2")

    for(i in 1:nlines){

      w<-sim_new(tau mu_g=mu_g_sim, b_M=b_M_sim, s2_M=s2_M_sim)

      res[i,"Ew"]<-mean(w)  # mean fitness of cells 

      P<-table(w)/N
      P<-P[-which(names(P)=="0")]

      res[i,"EP"]<-mean(P)    # mean colony size of mutations
      res[i,"EP2"]<-mean(P^2) # mean squared colony size of mutations
    }

    newsim[tau, "Ew"]<-mean(res[,"Ew"], na.rm=TRUE)   # mean fitness across lines 
    newsim[tau, "Vw"]<-var(res[,"Ew"], na.rm=TRUE)    # variance in fitness across lines
    newsim[tau, "EP"]<-mean(res[,"EP"], na.rm=TRUE)   # mean colony size across lines
    newsim[tau, "EP2"]<-mean(res[,"EP2"], na.rm=TRUE) # mean squared colony size across lines

    newsim<-as.data.frame(newsim)
}
```
</div>


```{r save_sim, eval=save, echo=FALSE}
if(rerun.newsim){
  save(newsim, file=file.path(root,'models/newsim.Rdata'))
}
```

We can plot the results of the simulation and overlay our theoretical predictions, which look adequate

```{r newsim_plot, fig.width = 7,fig.height = 7}

newsim$N<-2^newsim$tau

par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar=c(5, 5, 0.5, 2)+0.1, bty="l")

plot(Ew~tau, data=newsim, ylab=expression(beta[italic(M)]), xlab=expression(tau[s]), cex.lab=1.5)
lines(mu_g_sim*b_M_sim*log(N+1)~tau, data=newsim, col="red")
lines(mu_g_sim*b_M_sim*log(N, base=2)~tau, data=newsim, col="blue")

plot(Vw~tau, data=newsim, ylab=expression(sigma[italic(M)]^2), xlab=expression(tau[s]), cex.lab=1.5)
abline(h=mu_g_sim*(s2_M_sim+b_M_sim^2), col="red")
lines(mu_g_sim*(1-log(N+1)/N)*(s2_M_sim+b_M_sim^2)~tau, data=newsim, col="blue")

plot(EP~tau, data=newsim, ylab=expression(paste("E[", P, "]")), xlab=expression(tau[s]), cex.lab=1.5)
lines(log(N+1)/N~tau, data=newsim, col="red")

plot(EP2~tau, data=newsim, ylab=expression(paste("E[", P^2, "]")), xlab=expression(tau[s]), cex.lab=1.5)
lines(I((1/N)-log(N+1)/N^2)~tau, data=newsim, col="red")
```

## Bias correction

We do not know what the true values of $\beta_M$ and $\sigma^2_M$ but we do have estimates for them. However, these estimates will be biased when the number of putative mutations is not equal to the number of true mutations.  

Since we assume both the mean and between-line variance scale linearly with the number of mutations, we can get an approximate expression for the bias from linear-regression theory: $E[\widehat{\beta_M}] = \rho \beta_M$ and  $E[\widehat{\sigma^2_M}] = \rho \sigma^2_M$ where $\rho$ is the regression of the number of true mutations ($n^{(tp)}+n^{(fp)}$) on the number of putative mutations:

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rl}
\rho =& \frac{COV((1-\delta)(n^{(tp)}_{i}+n^{(fn)}_{i})+\delta(n^{(tp)}_{j}+n^{(fn)}_{j}), n^{(tp)}_{i}+n^{(fp)}_{i})}{VAR((1-\delta)(n^{(tp)}_{i}+n^{(fn)}_{i})+\delta(n^{(tp)}_{j}+n^{(fn)}_{j}))}\\
=& \frac{(1-p_M)VAR(n^{(tp)})}{VAR(n^{(tp)}+n^{(fn)})}\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}

Again, assuming the number of true-positives and false-negatives are independent and Poisson distributed this becomes:

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rl}
\rho =& \frac{(1-p_M)E[n^{(tp)}]}{E[n^{(tp)}]+E[n^{(fp)}]}\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}

We do not know the expected number of false-positives per line, but we expect it to be very low. Assuming it is the same as the expected false-negative rate we get $\rho$=`r round(rho, 4)`: the attenuation due to false-positives and mix-ups is modest. Note that the number of false-negatives do not appear in this expression because they introduce Berkson errors rather than classical errors and therefore do not result in slope attenuation \citep{Berkson.1950}.   



The expected between-line variance is 

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rl}
\sigma^2_L =&\rho(n^{(tp)}+n^{(fp)})\sigma^2_M+\mu_g(\beta_M^2+\sigma^2_M)+(E[n^{(fn)}]+p_mE[n^{(tp)}])(\beta_M^2+\sigma^2_M)+p_m(1-p_m)E[n^{(tp)}]^2\beta_M^2+\sigma^2_E\\

\sigma^2_L =&\left(\rho(n^{(tp)}+n^{(fp)})+E[n^{(fn)}]+p_mE[n^{(tp)}]+\mu_g\right)\sigma^2_M+\left(\mu_g+E[n^{(fn)}]+p_mE[n^{(tp)}]+p_m(1-p_m)E[n^{(tp)}]^2\right)\beta_M^2+\sigma^2_E\\

\end{array}
\end{equation}

The expected mean fitness is 

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rl}
\beta_L=&\beta_M(\rho(n^{(tp)}+n^{(fp)})+E[n^{(fn)}]+p_mE[n^{(tp)}]+\mu_g\tau)\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}

`m_correction` is a function that can fit this model using maximum-likelihood. The covariate $n$ ($n^{(tp)}+n^{(fp)}$) is replaced by $\rho(n^{(tp)}+n^{(fp)})+E[n^{(fn)}]+p_mE[n^{(tp)}]+\mu_g\tau$ in the fixed formula (with coefficient $\beta_M$) and by $\rho(n^{(tp)}+n^{(fp)})+E[n^{(fn)}]+p_mE[n^{(tp)}]+\mu_g$ in the random slope formula. An additional between-line variance component is included with the variance $\left(\mu_g+E[n^{(fn)}]+p_mE[n^{(tp)}]+p_m(1-p_m)E[n^{(tp)}]^2\right)\beta_M^2$. Conditional on $\beta_M$, the model is a standard linear-mixed model and the likelihood extracted. We fit the mixed model using glmmTMB since it allows variances to be fixed, unlike lmer. `optim` is used to select the $\beta_M$ that maximises the conditional likelihood.
   
<div class="fold s">
```{r m_correction}
library(glmmTMB)

m_correction<-function(formula, n, data, tau=tau, mu_g=mu_g, Etp=Etp, Efp=Efp, Efn=Efn, p_m=p_m){

  m1<-glmmTMB(formula,  data=data)

  ff<-as.character(formula)

  if(any(grepl("new_n|new_sqrtn|line2", ff))){
    stop("Sorry new_n, new_sqrtn and line2 are reserved, please rename these variables")
  }
  if(!"line"%in%colnames(data)){
    stop("Expecting a column 'line' in data")
  }

  ff<-gsub(paste0("\\ *\\+*\\ *", n, sep=""), "", ff)
  ff<-gsub("sqrt\\(\\)", "sqrt(new_n2)", ff)
  ff<-as.formula(paste(ff[c(2,1,3)], collapse=""))
  ff<-update(ff, .~new_n+(1|line2)+.)
  # add new_n as the first fixed predictor and line2 as the first set of random effects

  rho<-(1-p_m)*Etp/(Etp+Efp)

  data[,"new_n"]<-rho*data[,n]+Efn+p_m*Etp+mu_g*tau
   
  data[,"new_n2"]<-rho*data[,n]+mu_g+Efn+p_m*Etp

  data[,"line2"]<-data$line

  nLL<-function(par, data, m1, n, ff, mu_g, Etp, Efn, p_m, nLLonly=TRUE){

     bMbias<-(mu_g+Efn+p_m*Etp+p_m*(1-p_m)*(Etp^2))*par^2

     beta_start<-fixef(m1)$cond[-which(names(fixef(m1)$cond)==n)]
     beta_start<-c(beta_start[1], par, beta_start[-1])

     beta_map<-seq_along(beta_start)
     beta_map[2]<-NA
     beta_map<-as.factor(beta_map)

     theta_start<-c(log(sqrt(bMbias)), log(sqrt(unlist(VarCorr(m1)$cond))))

     theta_map<-seq_along(theta_start)
     theta_map[1]<-NA
     theta_map<-as.factor(theta_map)

     m2<-glmmTMB(ff,  data=data, REML=FALSE, start = list(beta=beta_start, theta = theta_start), map = list(beta=beta_map, theta = theta_map))

     if(nLLonly){
        return(m2$fit$objective)
     }else{
        return(m2)
     }
  }

  bM<-optim(par=fixef(m1)$cond[n], nLL, data=data, n=n, m1=m1, ff=ff, mu_g=mu_g, Etp=Etp, Efn=Efn, p_m=p_m, hessian=FALSE)$par

  return(nLL(par=bM, data=data, n=n, m1=m1, ff=ff, mu_g=mu_g, Etp=Etp, Efn=Efn, p_m=p_m, nLLonly=FALSE))
}
```
</div>


We can test how well this model recovers true values using simulation. We simulate data according to our experimental design, but substantially increase the error rates, mix-up rates at $\mu_g$: these values are so small in reality that the expected bias would be small and hard to detect (see below). We also use large values of $\beta_m$, $\sigma^2_M$ and $\sigma^2_E$ for the same reason: 

```{r }
mu_g_sim<-0.01
tau_sim<-20

b_M_sim<-0.5
s2_M_sim<-1
s2_E_sim<-0.5
s2_e_sim<-0.01

p_m_sim<-0.2
Etp_sim<-1
Efn_sim<-0.2
Efp_sim<-0.1
```

<div class="fold s">
```{r sim_correction, eval=rerun.estsim}
nlines<-188
nrep<-14
nsim<-500

estsim<-matrix(NA, nsim, 6)

colnames(estsim)<-c("b_M.1", "s2_E.1", "s2_M.1", "b_M.2", "s2_E.2", "s2_M.2")

for(i in 1:nsim){

  delta<-rbinom(nlines, size=1, prob=p_m_sim)

  nfn<-rpois(nlines, Efn_sim)
  ntp<-rpois(nlines, Etp_sim)
  nfp<-rpois(nlines, Efp_sim)

  nj<-rpois(nlines, Etp_sim+Efp_sim)    # Observed mutations given a mix-up

  n_true<-ntp+nfn                       # True mutations 
  n_obs<-(1-delta)*(ntp+nfp)+delta*nj   # Observed mutations   

  line_mean<-unlist(lapply(sapply(n_true, rnorm, mean=b_M_sim, sd=sqrt(s2_M_sim)), sum)) 
  # effect of true mutations
  line_mean<-line_mean+rnorm(nlines, 0, sqrt(s2_E_sim))
  # effect of line environment

  for(j in 1:nlines){
    line_mean<-line_mean+mean(sim_new(tau_sim, mu_g_sim, b_M_sim, s2_M_sim))
    # add the contribution of new mutations
  }

  y<-sapply(line_mean, function(x){rnorm(nrep, x, sqrt(s2_e_sim))})
  # generate nrep replicates per line and add noise

  dat<-data.frame(y=c(y), line=as.factor(rep(1:nlines, each=nrep)), n_obs=rep(n_obs, each=nrep))

  m1.sim<-glmmTMB(y~n_obs+(1|line)+(sqrt(n_obs)-1|line), data=dat)

  m2.sim<-m_correction(y~n_obs+(1|line)+(sqrt(n_obs)-1|line), n="n_obs", data=dat, tau=tau, mu_g=mu_g, Etp=Etp, Efp=Efp, Efn=Efn, p_m=p_m)

  estsim[i,]<-c(fixef(m1.sim)$cond["n_obs"], unlist(VarCorr(m1.sim)$cond), fixef(m2.sim)$cond["new_n"], unlist(VarCorr(m2.sim)$cond)[c("line", "line.1")])

  print(i)

}
```
</div>

```{r save_sim2, eval=save, echo=FALSE}

  save(estsim, file=file.path(root,'models/estsim.Rdata'))
}
```

```

We can start by plotting the naive estimates, with true values in blue and their expected (biased) values in red and observed means in black:


```{r estsim_plot1, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 12}
rho_sim<-(1-p_m_sim)*Etp_sim/(Etp_sim+Efp_sim)

par(mfrow=c(3,1))
hist(estsim[,"b_M.1"], xlab=expression(widehat(beta[M])), main="", breaks=50)
abline(v=b_M_sim, col="blue")
abline(v=mean(estsim[,"b_M.1"]))
abline(v=rho_sim*b_M_sim, col="red")

hist(estsim[,"s2_M.1"], xlab=expression(widehat(sigma[M]^2)), main="", breaks=50)
abline(v=s2_M_sim, col="blue")
abline(v=mean(estsim[,"s2_M.1"]))
abline(v=rho_sim*s2_M_sim, col="red")

hist(estsim[,"s2_E.1"], xlab=expression(widehat(sigma[E]^2)), main="", breaks=50)
abline(v=s2_E_sim, col="blue")
abline(v=mean(estsim[,"s2_E.1"]))
abline(v=s2_E_sim+(b_M_sim^2+s2_M_sim)*(mu_g_sim+Efn_sim+p_m_sim*Etp_sim)+p_m_sim*(1-p_m_sim)*(Etp_sim^2)*b_M_sim^2, col="red")
```

There are substantial biases in the estimates and these are well predicted by our theoretical expectations. We can also look at the estimates from the model that tries to accommodate mutation calling errors, mix-ups and new mutations. Again, we plot the true values in blue, the expected `naive' biased estimator in red and the mean of the estimates in black.  

```{r estsim_plot2, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 12}
par(mfrow=c(3,1))
hist(estsim[,"b_M.2"], breaks=30, xlab=expression(widehat(beta[M])), main="")
abline(v=b_M_sim, col="blue")
abline(v=mean(estsim[,"b_M.2"]))
abline(v=rho_sim*b_M_sim, col="red")

hist(estsim[,"s2_M.2"], breaks=30, xlab=expression(widehat(sigma[M]^2)), main="")
abline(v=s2_M_sim, col="blue")
abline(v=mean(estsim[,"s2_M.2"]))
abline(v=rho_sim*s2_M_sim, col="red")

hist(estsim[,"s2_E.2"], breaks=30, xlab=expression(widehat(sigma[E]^2)), main="")
abline(v=s2_E_sim, col="blue")
abline(v=mean(estsim[,"s2_E.2"]))
abline(v=s2_E_sim+(b_M_sim^2+s2_M_sim)*(mu_g_sim+Efn_sim+p_m_sim*Etp_sim)+p_m_sim*(1-p_m_sim)*(Etp_sim^2)*b_M_sim^2, col="red")

```

The corrected estimates look unbiased for $\beta_M$ and $\sigma^2_M$. While the estimate for $\sigma^2_E$ is substantially better, some slight overestimation is observed, but this is likely due to many estimates been bound at zero rather than a problem with the model: no non-negative estimator of a random-effect variance is known. 

We  can apply these models to our own data, but using our empirically assessed error rate parameters:

```{r }
m1_correct<-m_correction(r~mutation + anc + person + inner + (noanc-1|line) + (sqrt(mutation)-1|line) + (1|plate) + (1|plate:column) + (1|plate:row), n="mutation", data=df, tau=tau, mu_g=mu_g, Etp=Etp, Efp=Efp, Efn=Efn, p_m=p_m)

summary(m1_correct)
```

The estimate of $\sigma^2_E$ has hardly shifted, and is `r round(VarCorr(m1_correct)$line/VarCorr(m1)$line,5)` times its original value. $\sigma^2_E$ remains significantly different from zero, although the p-value is less extreme: 

```{r }
m6_correct<-m_correction(r~mutation + anc + person + inner + (sqrt(mutation)-1|line) + (1|plate) + (1|plate:column) + (1|plate:row), n="mutation", data=df, tau=tau, mu_g=mu_g, Etp=Etp, Efp=Efp, Efn=Efn, p_m=p_m)

anova(m1_correct, m6_correct)
```
